{{Short description|Spatial correlation measure}}
'''Lee's ''L''''' is a bivariate spatial [[correlation coefficient]] which measures the association between two sets of observations made at the same spatial sites. Standard measures of [[Correlation|association]] such as the [[Pearson correlation coefficient]] do not account for the spatial dimension of data, in particular they are vulnerable to inflation due to spatial [[autocorrelation]]. Lee's ''L'' is available in numerous [[spatial analysis]] software libraries including ''spdep'' <ref>{{cite web | url=https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/reference/lee.test.html | title=Lee's L test for spatial autocorrelation — lee.test }}</ref> and [[PySAL]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pysal.org/esda/api.html | title=API reference — esda v0.1.dev1+ga296c39 Manual }}</ref> (where it is called ''Spatial_Pearson'') and has been applied in diverse applications such as studying [[air pollution]],<ref>

== Formula ==
For spatial data <math>x_i</math> and <math>y_i</math> measured at <math>N</math> locations connected with the spatial weight matrix <math>w_{ij}</math> first define the spatially lagged vector

:<math>\tilde{x}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j</math>

with a similar definition for <math>\tilde{y}_i</math>. Then Lee's ''L''<ref name="lee">
{{Cite journal
 | doi = 10.1007/s101090100064
 | first1 = Sang-Il
 | last1 = Lee
 | year = 2001
 | title =Developing a bivariate spatial association measure: an integration of Pearson's r and Moran's I. 
 | journal = Journal of Geographical Systems
 | volume = 3
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 369–385
| bibcode = 2001JGS.....3..369L
 }}
</ref> is defined as

:<math>
L_{x,y} = \frac{N}{\sum_i \left( \sum_j w_{ij} \right)^2} \frac{\sum_{ij} (\tilde{x}_i - \bar{x})(\tilde{y}_i - \bar{y}) }{ \sqrt{ \sum_i (\tilde{x}_i - \bar{x})^2} \sqrt{ \sum_i (\tilde{y}_i - \bar{y})^2} }
</math>

where <math>\bar{x}, \bar{y}</math> are the mean values of <math>x_i, y_i</math>. When the spatial weight matrix is row normalized, such that <math>\sum_j w_{ij} = 1</math>, the first factor is 1.

=== Alternate definition ===
Lee also defines the ''spatial smoothing scalar''
:<math>
SSS_{x} = \frac{ \sum_i (\tilde{x}_i - \bar{x})^2}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
</math>
to measure the spatial [[autocorrelation]] of a variable.

It is shown by Lee<ref name="lee" /> that the above definition is equivalent to
:<math>
L_{x,y} = \sqrt{ SSS_{x} } \sqrt{ SSS_{y} } r( \tilde{x}, \tilde{y} )
</math>
Where <math>r</math> is the [[Pearson correlation coefficient]]
:<math>
r(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}) =\frac{\sum ^n _{i=1}(\tilde{x}_i - \bar{\tilde{x}})(\tilde{y}_i - \bar{\tilde{y}})}{\sqrt{\sum ^n _{i=1}(\tilde{x}_i - \bar{\tilde{x}})^2} \sqrt{\sum ^n _{i=1}(\tilde{y}_i - \bar{\tilde{y}})^2}}
</math>
This means Lee's L is equivalent to the Pearson correlation of the spatially lagged data, multiplied by a measure of each data set's spatial autocorrelation.
